screens.title: Advanced Contract Interaction Patterns & Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: In this module we'll focus on the practical techniques that keep a dApp responsive and secure when interacting with smart contracts. You will learn how to parse and present clear error messages from failed transactions, how to batch view calls to cut network latency, and how to apply optimistic UI updates so users see immediate feedback while the chain confirms changes. We'll also cover patterns for managing multiple contract instances in a single component and front-end security measures like input validation, sanitization, and network verification. For example, when a transaction reverts you can parse the revert reason and show a specific message instead of a generic failure line. When fetching several view values, bundling them with BatchRequest reduces round trips and improves load time. And when you optimistically update a counter before a transaction is mined, you must store the previous state to roll back on failure. Each screen below combines a short code example or pattern, a concrete scenario, a misconception to watch for, and a takeaway you can apply immediately. By the end you should be able to implement robust error parsing, use BatchRequest effectively, add optimistic updates safely, and harden your front-end against common mistakes. Where could you apply these patterns in your own dApp?

screens.title: Robust Error Handling for call() and send()
screens.narratorSegment: Robust error handling starts with recognizing where errors originate and giving the user a clear next step. Errors can come from the wallet (user rejection), the node (network timeouts), insufficient funds, or the contract itself (revert or require). A common mistake is treating every error the same — a generic alert leaves users confused. Instead, inspect the error. message and classify it. For example, if the message includes user denial, explain that the signature was rejected and suggest retrying. If it mentions insufficient funds, instruct the user to add Ether for gas. If the message contains revert, attempt to extract the revert reason using a regular expression; many providers include the Solidity revert message when compiled with versions that preserve it. Remember that parsing can be provider-dependent, so fallback gracefully to a generic message and log the full error for debugging. A best practice is to centralize error normalization in one utility function so UI components only consume clear, categorized failures. Concrete example: in a send try/catch, examine error. message for the strings "User denied transaction signature", "insufficient funds", and "revert"; map each to a user-facing sentence and an internal error code. A common misconception is that call() cannot fail — view calls still fail if the node is unreachable, the address is invalid, or the function itself uses require. Close by asking: what is the most common error your dApp encounters and how would you normalize it for users?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Error Handling
Definition

Robust Error Handling

Classify and convert provider errors into concise user actions and rollback steps. Avoid vague messages.

Common classes
  • Wallet rejections — ask user to approve the tx
  • Insufficient funds — show gas estimate and top-up advice
  • Reverts — parse revert reason when available
  • Network errors — retry/backoff and show status
Misconception

Not all errors include meaningful text. Treat parsing as best-effort and always provide a fallback message with a support link or retry option.

Key Takeaway

Normalize provider errors into user actions and centralize parsing to avoid scattered logic across components.

Example — parse transaction errors
try {
  await myContract.methods.doSomething().send({ from: accounts[0] });
} catch (error) {
  if (error.message.includes("User denied transaction signature")) {
    setError("Transaction rejected by user in MetaMask.");
  } else if (error.message.includes("insufficient funds")) {
    setError("Insufficient Ether in your wallet for gas.");
  } else if (error.message.includes("revert")) {
    const match = error.message.match(/revert: (.*)/);
    const reason = match ? match[1] : "Transaction reverted without specific reason.";
    setError(`Transaction failed: ${reason}`);
  } else {
    setError(`An unexpected error occurred: ${error.message}`);
  }
  console.error("Transaction error:", error);
}
Store a previous state when you optimistically update, and always revert to it if the normalized error indicates a failed transaction. Centralized utilities make this straightforward to reuse across the app.

screens.title: Handling Transaction Reverts Effectively
screens.narratorSegment: Transaction reverts are a common source of confusion for users. When a contract uses require or revert, a failed send may return a message that contains the revert text, but this depends on the Solidity version and the RPC provider. Start by attempting to parse the error. message for a revert reason with a regex; if present, show it to the user as a concrete cause. If the revert reason suggests incorrect inputs, point the user to correct form fields. If it cites a contract invariant or a business rule, explain that the action is not permitted and suggest alternatives. For provider-dependent cases, add a secondary strategy: perform a simulated call using call() with identical inputs before sending; many developers use this as a preflight check because calls execute locally and will return revert reasons without spending gas. However, be aware that some state changes or nonce ordering can cause differences, so treat simulation as a helpful but not perfect pre-check. A common misconception is that a revert reason always guarantees precise debugging — sometimes the reason is generic or absent. Always provide a fallback message and log the full error for developers. Closing question: how would you decide when to run a simulation call versus relying on post-failure parsing?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Transaction Reverts
Process

Revert handling flow

1. Simulate with call()
Run the same function as a call to surface potential revert reasons without gas cost.
2. Send transaction
If simulation passes, send the transaction with a gas buffer; otherwise, show the revert reason and halt.
3. Parse post-failure
If the tx reverts, extract a reason from error.message when present and explain necessary fixes.
Key Takeaway

Simulation + revert parsing together give the best UX; but always include fallbacks and clear user guidance.

Example — simulation before send
// simulate with call to surface revert
try {
  await contract.methods.doSomething(arg).call({ from: accounts[0] });
} catch (simErr) {
  // show simulation error as actionable feedback
  setError(`Preflight failed: ${simErr.message}`);
  return;
}

// if simulation passed, proceed to send
try {
  await contract.methods.doSomething(arg).send({ from: accounts[0] });
} catch (err) {
  // parse revert reason like earlier example
  console.error('Send failed', err);
}
Note: simulation may not catch issues caused by state changes between call and send or by miner behavior, but it is a lightweight preflight that improves UX in many cases.

screens.title: call() vs send() — Failure Modes and UX
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between call and send is crucial for both UX and error handling. call() executes a function locally on a node and returns results without consuming gas; it's safe and fast for reads but can still fail if the node is unreachable, the contract address is wrong, or the view function contains require statements. Because call() does not change chain state, you can use it for preflight simulations. send() creates an on-chain transaction that consumes gas, may be rejected by the wallet, and can revert due to contract logic. UX-wise, call failures should trigger retry and network checks, whereas send failures need more careful user guidance, gas estimation, and rollback strategies if you used optimistic updates. A common misconception is that call() results are guaranteed to match subsequent transaction outcomes; nonce ordering, state changes by other actors, or gas-dependent reverts can lead to differences. Therefore treat call() as a helpful check but always prepare for send failures. Example: use call() to read a balance and to run a quick simulation, but always estimate gas and parse send errors before confirming state in the UI. How would you present to a user the difference in expected behavior between reads and state changes?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › call() vs send()
call()

Read-only / Simulation

  • No gas used, executes locally on a node.
  • Useful for preflight checks and fetching state.
  • Can fail if node unreachable or function contains require.
UI action: retry, show network status, use as helpful simulation but not as ground truth for state changes.
send()

State-changing transaction

  • Consumes gas and requires wallet signature.
  • May be rejected by user or revert due to contract logic.
  • Requires gas estimation and rollback if using optimistic UI.
UI action: estimate gas, parse reverts, show clear confirmation and rollback plan on failure.

screens.title: BatchRequest: Bundle multiple call() requests
screens.narratorSegment: BatchRequest is a simple performance multiplier for dApps that need several values at load time. Rather than issuing separate HTTP calls for each view, create a web3. BatchRequest and add each contract. methods. x(). call. request to it with callbacks that store results. When you execute the batch the node handles all calls in one request, reducing round-trip latency and improving perceived load speed. Use BatchRequest in initial data loads such as fetching a user's token balance, NFT count, and contract status message at once. Important detail: you need access to the web3 instance to construct the batch, and callbacks must safely mutate local variables or set state after execute completes. A common pitfall is assuming callbacks run synchronously; collect results in outer-scoped variables and update React state only after batch. execute(). Also handle errors inside each callback to avoid silent failures. In the CounterApp example, fetching getCount and getOwner via a single batch yields a single network call and fewer re-renders. Ask yourself: which combinations of contract reads in your app are best bundled into a batch to improve initial load time?

keyIdea.title: Bundle reads
keyIdea.text: Use web3.BatchRequest to minimize RPC calls when loading multiple view values, and update state after batch completion.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › BatchRequest

When to batch

Batch reads that are required together for a single render to reduce latency and re-renders.

Pattern
  1. Create new web3.BatchRequest()
  2. Add .call.request() items with callbacks
  3. await batch.execute(); then update state
Batch example
const batch = new web3.BatchRequest();
let results = {};

batch.add(myContract.methods.getCount().call.request({}, (err, data) => {
  if (!err) results.count = parseInt(data);
  else console.error('Error fetching count:', err);
}));

batch.add(myContract.methods.getOwner().call.request({}, (err, data) => {
  if (!err) results.owner = data;
  else console.error('Error fetching owner:', err);
}));

await batch.execute();
setCount(results.count);
setOwner(results.owner);
Note: add error handling per-callback and update state only after execute to keep UI consistent.

screens.title: Implementing BatchRequest in a React CounterApp
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating BatchRequest into React requires careful attention to dependencies and state updates. In the chapter's CounterApp example we create a web3. BatchRequest and add two call. request items for getCount and getOwner. Important details: store intermediate results in local variables instead of calling setState inside each callback to avoid many re-renders and race conditions. After awaiting batch. execute(), update React state once with the collected results. Also, include web3 and contract as dependencies in useCallback and useEffect so changes to the provider or contract trigger a fresh fetch. Error handling inside each callback ensures one failed call doesn't block others; log per-call errors and present a single aggregated UI message if needed. Finally, guard against stale closures by checking that the component is still mounted before calling setState after the batch. A common error is forgetting to include the web3 instance in dependencies, which causes an out-of-date batch or runtime exceptions. In practice, this pattern reduces network overhead and accelerates component rendering when multiple reads are required. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Batch in React

fetchData using BatchRequest

Use web3.BatchRequest inside a useCallback, include web3 and contract in dependencies, and update state once.

const fetchData = useCallback(async () => {
  if (contract && web3) {
    try {
      const batch = new web3.BatchRequest();
      let fetchedCount = 0;
      let fetchedOwner = '';

      batch.add(contract.methods.getCount().call.request({}, (err, data) => {
        if (err) console.error('Batch error fetching count:', err);
        else fetchedCount = parseInt(data);
      }));

      batch.add(contract.methods.getOwner().call.request({}, (err, data) => {
        if (err) console.error('Batch error fetching owner:', err);
        else fetchedOwner = data;
      }));

      await batch.execute();

      setCount(fetchedCount);
      setOwner(fetchedOwner);
      setError('');
    } catch (err) {
      setError(`Error fetching data: ${err.message}`);
      console.error('Error fetching data:', err);
    }
  }
}, [contract, web3]);
Pro tip
Avoid setState in callbacks; update once after execute to minimize rerenders.
Common mistake
Forgetting to include web3 in dependencies can cause stale batches or runtime errors when provider changes.

screens.title: Optimistic UI Updates — Pattern and Safeguards
screens.narratorSegment: Optimistic UI updates improve perceived responsiveness by assuming a successful outcome and updating the UI immediately. The pattern requires storing the previous state, applying the optimistic change, sending the transaction, and then reverting if the transaction fails. Start by capturing the current state — for example, previousCount — then set the optimistic state like previousCount + 1. Show an explicit loading or pending indicator so the user understands the action is awaiting confirmation. Estimate gas and send the transaction in a try block. If it succeeds, you may either keep the optimistic state or re-fetch authoritative values after confirmation. If it fails, restore the previous state and display a normalized error. A common pitfall is not reserving gas margin: always add a buffer when submitting gas to reduce out-of-gas failures. Another pitfall is optimistic updates for complex multi-step processes where other actors can change state between optimistic update and confirmation; in those cases prefer conservative UI changes or event-driven confirmations. Example: incrementCountOptimistic stores prevCount, sets count to prevCount + 1, tries to send, and on catch restores prevCount. Ask yourself: what UI affordances reassure a user that an optimistic change might still fail?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Optimistic UI

Optimistic Update Steps

  1. Store previous state for rollback.
  2. Apply optimistic UI change and show pending indicator.
  3. Estimate gas, send tx with buffer, await result.
  4. On success, confirm or re-fetch; on failure, rollback and show error.
UX note
Make pending state explicit so users understand the action is provisional.
Optimistic increment example
const prevCount = count;
setCount(prevCount + 1);
setLoading(true);
try {
  const gasEstimate = await contract.methods.increment().estimateGas({ from: accounts[0] });
  await contract.methods.increment().send({ from: accounts[0], gas: gasEstimate + 10000 });
  // success: keep optimistic state or re-fetch after event
} catch (err) {
  setCount(prevCount); // rollback
  setError(`Transaction failed: ${err.message}`);
} finally {
  setLoading(false);
}
Remember to store prev state and to present a clear pending indicator. For complex state, consider event subscriptions rather than optimistic updates.

screens.title: Interacting with Multiple Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Most real dApps interact with several contracts: a core dApp contract, a token contract, and an NFT contract, for example. The pattern is straightforward: import ABIs, instantiate web3. eth. Contract for each address, and store them in component state or a context provider for shared use. Managing dependencies matters: useEffect hooks that depend on contract instances should list them explicitly so data fetches run when a contract changes. Keep instantiation logic centralized, for instance in an initWeb3 or contracts factory function, to avoid recreating contracts and causing stale references. When multiple contracts are required for a single render, combine their reads using BatchRequest where possible to reduce load time. Also be mindful of ordering: if contract A calls contract B on-chain, your UI should reflect that relationship; load the authoritative source first or show a loading dependency. A common mistake is creating circular useEffect triggers by setting state inside an effect that also depends on that state — avoid this by carefully planning dependencies and using useCallback. Example: create tokenContract and nftContract in initWeb3, set them in state, then use a fetchData effect that depends on both contracts and the accounts list. How will you structure your contract factory to avoid re-instantiation on every render?

Pattern

Example instantiation

Ensure your fetch effects run when contract or account changes. Use useCallback for functions that the effects call to avoid unnecessary re-runs.
Common mistake
Recreating contract instances on every render causes stale closures and performance issues. Create once and reuse.

screens.title: Frontend Security Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Frontend security for dApps focuses on protecting users and preventing common mistakes. Start with input validation: check types, ranges, and required fields in the UI before sending them to a contract. This prevents predictable revert errors and avoids wasting gas. Second, sanitize any on-chain string or metadata before inserting it into the DOM to avoid XSS vulnerabilities — assume on-chain data is untrusted. Third, never request or store private keys in the frontend; always rely on injected wallets for signing. Fourth, verify that the user's wallet is on the expected chain and show a prominent warning when it is not. Fifth, be aware of gas limit manipulation; estimate gas, add a safety buffer, and educate users about unusually high gas. A misconception is that backend or contract validation removes the need for frontend checks; while contracts should re-validate, frontend validation reduces bad UX and limits attack surface. In practice, combine validation, sanitization, and clear warnings to make interactions safer and less error-prone. What frontend check would prevent your most common transaction failure? Frontend Security Considerations means treat on-chain data as untrusted, validate inputs before sending, and never handle private keys in the frontend.. In practical terms, input validation, sanitization, network checks, and private-key safety. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Input Validation

Validate addresses, numeric ranges, and required fields before sending transactions to avoid reverts and wasted gas.

Sanitization

Escape or sanitize any user-generated on-chain content before rendering to prevent XSS.

Private Keys

Never ask for or store private keys in the frontend; use injected wallets like MetaMask for signing.

Verify chainId and estimate gas with a buffer. Warn users if they're on the wrong network or gas looks abnormal.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: When developing contract interaction code, several recurring mistakes cause bugs and poor UX. First, updating UI state inside each batch callback leads to many re-renders and race conditions. Instead, aggregate results and set state once. Second, forgetting to include web3 or contract in useEffect dependencies causes stale closures and missed updates — be explicit about dependencies. Third, relying solely on revert parsing without providing fallbacks is brittle; always include a generic error and developer logs. Fourth, skipping gas estimation or not adding a buffer can lead to out-of-gas failures; estimate and add a modest margin. Fifth, over-optimistic UI updates without a stored rollback state can leave the UI inconsistent on failure. Finally, neglecting to sanitize on-chain strings risks XSS. Best practices: centralize error normalization, batch reads where it matters, show pending states for optimistic updates, and validate inputs on the frontend. A short checklist before release: test user rejection flows, test revert parsing with a demo revert, validate BatchRequest behavior on your RPC provider, and confirm network verification works across wallets. Which of these mistakes have you encountered and how will you fix it?

fullNarratorScript:
In this module we'll focus on the practical techniques that keep a dApp responsive and secure when interacting with smart contracts. You will learn how to parse and present clear error messages from failed transactions, how to batch view calls to cut network latency, and how to apply optimistic UI updates so users see immediate feedback while the chain confirms changes. We'll also cover patterns for managing multiple contract instances in a single component and front-end security measures like input validation, sanitization, and network verification. For example, when a transaction reverts you can parse the revert reason and show a specific message instead of a generic failure line. When fetching several view values, bundling them with BatchRequest reduces round trips and improves load time. And when you optimistically update a counter before a transaction is mined, you must store the previous state to roll back on failure. Each screen below combines a short code example or pattern, a concrete scenario, a misconception to watch for, and a takeaway you can apply immediately. By the end you should be able to implement robust error parsing, use BatchRequest effectively, add optimistic updates safely, and harden your front-end against common mistakes. Where could you apply these patterns in your own dApp?

By the end of this chapter you will implement focused, testable skills that improve both reliability and experience in a dApp. First, you will be able to implement robust error handling for send and call operations, parsing common messages like user rejections, insufficient funds, and revert reasons so users receive helpful guidance. Second, you will learn how to batch multiple view calls using Web3. js BatchRequest to reduce network latency when your UI needs several values at once. Third, you will apply optimistic UI updates to make state changes feel immediate while still providing a safe rollback if a transaction fails. Finally, you will set up and manage multiple contract instances in a single component without creating awkward dependency cycles. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a milestone so you can verify competency while building your CounterApp use case.

This second objectives slide focuses on the security and operational edge cases you'll need to manage. You will learn how to validate inputs before they reach a contract to prevent unnecessary gas expenditure and improve UX. You will implement display sanitization to reduce the risk of XSS when showing user-provided blockchain data, for example NFT metadata or profile text stored on-chain. You will also verify the user's network to avoid accidental transactions on the wrong chain, and communicate gas limit risks to users so they can make informed choices. Finally, you'll learn to handle provider-level network errors with retry strategies so transient node outages don't break your UI. Each card contains a small mnemonic and a milestone so you can demonstrate the behavior in your CounterApp by deliberately failing and recovering a transaction or by showing a sanitized UI string.

Robust error handling starts with recognizing where errors originate and giving the user a clear next step. Errors can come from the wallet (user rejection), the node (network timeouts), insufficient funds, or the contract itself (revert or require). A common mistake is treating every error the same — a generic alert leaves users confused. Instead, inspect the error. message and classify it. For example, if the message includes user denial, explain that the signature was rejected and suggest retrying. If it mentions insufficient funds, instruct the user to add Ether for gas. If the message contains revert, attempt to extract the revert reason using a regular expression; many providers include the Solidity revert message when compiled with versions that preserve it. Remember that parsing can be provider-dependent, so fallback gracefully to a generic message and log the full error for debugging. A best practice is to centralize error normalization in one utility function so UI components only consume clear, categorized failures. Concrete example: in a send try/catch, examine error. message for the strings "User denied transaction signature", "insufficient funds", and "revert"; map each to a user-facing sentence and an internal error code. A common misconception is that call() cannot fail — view calls still fail if the node is unreachable, the address is invalid, or the function itself uses require. Close by asking: what is the most common error your dApp encounters and how would you normalize it for users?

Transaction reverts are a common source of confusion for users. When a contract uses require or revert, a failed send may return a message that contains the revert text, but this depends on the Solidity version and the RPC provider. Start by attempting to parse the error. message for a revert reason with a regex; if present, show it to the user as a concrete cause. If the revert reason suggests incorrect inputs, point the user to correct form fields. If it cites a contract invariant or a business rule, explain that the action is not permitted and suggest alternatives. For provider-dependent cases, add a secondary strategy: perform a simulated call using call() with identical inputs before sending; many developers use this as a preflight check because calls execute locally and will return revert reasons without spending gas. However, be aware that some state changes or nonce ordering can cause differences, so treat simulation as a helpful but not perfect pre-check. A common misconception is that a revert reason always guarantees precise debugging — sometimes the reason is generic or absent. Always provide a fallback message and log the full error for developers. Closing question: how would you decide when to run a simulation call versus relying on post-failure parsing?

Understanding the difference between call and send is crucial for both UX and error handling. call() executes a function locally on a node and returns results without consuming gas; it's safe and fast for reads but can still fail if the node is unreachable, the contract address is wrong, or the view function contains require statements. Because call() does not change chain state, you can use it for preflight simulations. send() creates an on-chain transaction that consumes gas, may be rejected by the wallet, and can revert due to contract logic. UX-wise, call failures should trigger retry and network checks, whereas send failures need more careful user guidance, gas estimation, and rollback strategies if you used optimistic updates. A common misconception is that call() results are guaranteed to match subsequent transaction outcomes; nonce ordering, state changes by other actors, or gas-dependent reverts can lead to differences. Therefore treat call() as a helpful check but always prepare for send failures. Example: use call() to read a balance and to run a quick simulation, but always estimate gas and parse send errors before confirming state in the UI. How would you present to a user the difference in expected behavior between reads and state changes?

BatchRequest is a simple performance multiplier for dApps that need several values at load time. Rather than issuing separate HTTP calls for each view, create a web3. BatchRequest and add each contract. methods. x(). call. request to it with callbacks that store results. When you execute the batch the node handles all calls in one request, reducing round-trip latency and improving perceived load speed. Use BatchRequest in initial data loads such as fetching a user's token balance, NFT count, and contract status message at once. Important detail: you need access to the web3 instance to construct the batch, and callbacks must safely mutate local variables or set state after execute completes. A common pitfall is assuming callbacks run synchronously; collect results in outer-scoped variables and update React state only after batch. execute(). Also handle errors inside each callback to avoid silent failures. In the CounterApp example, fetching getCount and getOwner via a single batch yields a single network call and fewer re-renders. Ask yourself: which combinations of contract reads in your app are best bundled into a batch to improve initial load time?

BatchRequest and add two call. request items for getCount and getOwner. Important details: store intermediate results in local variables instead of calling setState inside each callback to avoid many re-renders and race conditions. After awaiting batch. execute(), update React state once with the collected results. Also, include web3 and contract as dependencies in useCallback and useEffect so changes to the provider or contract trigger a fresh fetch. Finally, guard against stale closures by checking that the component is still mounted before calling setState after the batch. Optimistic UI updates improve perceived responsiveness by assuming a successful outcome and updating the UI immediately. The pattern requires storing the previous state, applying the optimistic change, sending the transaction, and then reverting if the transaction fails. Start by capturing the current state — for example, previousCount — then set the optimistic state like previousCount + 1. Show an explicit loading or pending indicator so the user understands the action is awaiting confirmation. Estimate gas and send the transaction in a try block. If it succeeds, you may either keep the optimistic state or re-fetch authoritative values after confirmation. If it fails, restore the previous state and display a normalized error. A common pitfall is not reserving gas margin: always add a buffer when submitting gas to reduce out-of-gas failures. Another pitfall is optimistic updates for complex multi-step processes where other actors can change state between optimistic update and confirmation; in those cases prefer conservative UI changes or event-driven confirmations. Example: incrementCountOptimistic stores prevCount, sets count to prevCount + 1, tries to send, and on catch restores prevCount. When developing contract interaction code, several recurring mistakes cause bugs and poor UX. First, updating UI state inside each batch callback leads to many re-renders and race conditions. Instead, aggregate results and set state once. Second, forgetting to include web3 or contract in useEffect dependencies causes stale closures and missed updates — be explicit about dependencies. Third, relying solely on revert parsing without providing fallbacks is brittle; always include a generic error and developer logs. Fourth, skipping gas estimation or not adding a buffer can lead to out-of-gas failures; estimate and add a modest margin. Fifth, over-optimistic UI updates without a stored rollback state can leave the UI inconsistent on failure. Finally, neglecting to sanitize on-chain strings risks XSS. Best practices: centralize error normalization, batch reads where it matters, show pending states for optimistic updates, and validate inputs on the frontend. Third, BatchRequest bundles multiple view calls into a single RPC request which reduces latency and improves perceived performance.
